endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: This control requires establishing a centralized monitoring mechanism - such as a dashboard or equivalent reporting interface - that enables frequent review of key performance, utilization, and bias indicators, and flags unexpected or out-of-scope usage patterns for manual review by IT, compliance, and other designated oversight functions.

endorsements.title: FUTURE-AI: international consensus guideline for trustworthy and deployable artificial intelligence in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Customise training to all end user groups

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: For this step, the team should determine whether there is a training curriculum and related materials for the AI solution, and if so, whether it provides for training for specialized roles.

endorsements.title: Stakeholder-centric participation in large language models enhanced health systems
endorsements.quote: By offering tailored learning modules specific to different roles and simulating healthcare scenarios, LLMs can facilitate hands-on practice that deepens understanding and builds confidence 63 .

endorsements.title: Hype vs Reality in the Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Workflows
endorsements.quote: Health care institutions should complement academic reform with ongoing, role-specific professional training that balances theoretical understanding with hands-on experience.

endorsements.title: From promising prototypes to "instructions for use": embedding LLMs safely in perioperative and intensive care
endorsements.issuer: Journal of clinical monitoring and computing
endorsements.quote: Role-specific competencies are also needed: bedside nurses should learn to recognise when LLM-generated triage suggestions conflict with direct observation and how to escalate; residents and fellows should practise integrating outputs into care plans and handovers; consultants and leaders should be equipped to interpret dashboards, participate in governance, and mentor junior staff.

evidence.title: Increasing Advance Care Planning Discussions and Documentation
evidence.venue: Journal of the advanced practitioner in oncology
evidence.outcome: ACP discussion documentation after provider education on the mortality-alert response workflow
evidence.effect: Documentation increased from three of eight patients (37.5%) before education to three of seven (42.9%) afterward; p =.999. All documented ACP discussions used bookends.
evidence.quote: As seen in Figure 1 , out of the eight patients in the pre-education group, three (37.5%) had an ACP conversation documented, compared to three out of seven (42.9%) in the post-education group, which was not significantly different ( p =.999).

evidence.title: Improving Nurses' Management of Uterine Tachysystole
evidence.venue: MCN. The American journal of maternal child nursing
evidence.outcome: Timely tachysystole management, tachysystole incidence, and prolonged alerts after nurse education
evidence.effect: Education improved timely management with Category II/III fetal heart rate patterns (p < .001), but not tachysystole incidence among all births (p = .945), incidence with Category II/III patterns (p = .070), or prolonged alerts (p = .377).
evidence.quote: Phase II found a significant improvement in the timely management of tachysystole with evidence-based intervention in the presence of Category II/III fetal heart rate pattern ( p < .001).

evidence.title: Quantifying the AI readiness gap: An international, multidisciplinary assessment of artificial intelligence literacy in the radiation oncology community
evidence.outcome: Role-specific differences in AI knowledge scores among staff
evidence.effect: Medical Physicists scored higher than Radiation Oncologists and Radiation Therapists (p < 0.001); required competencies vary by role.
evidence.quote: Significant role-specific disparities emerged: Medical Physicists demonstrated higher scores than Radiation Oncologists and Radiation Therapists (p < 0.001).
evidence.sample_unit: respondents completing all items of the AI literacy assessment

commentary.bottom_line: Two small before-and-after studies of role-specific education for staff responding to AI alerts found mixed results, with one process measure improving and patient-level outcomes unchanged. The evidence cannot show whether tailoring training to roles performs better than generic training or no training.

perspectives.view: Both tests are uncontrolled pre-post designs in single deployments, one with 15 patients. Neither compared role-tailored training with generic training, which weakens directness. Results were inconsistent across outcomes, and the small samples make estimates imprecise. Certainty is very low. Secular trends or alert tuning could explain the nurse findings.

After nurse education, timely management of tachysystole with Category II/III fetal heart rate patterns improved (p < .001). Tachysystole incidence (p = .945) and prolonged alerts (p = .377) did not change. Training may change how staff respond to an alert without yet reducing the harm the alert is meant to prevent.

Provider education on a mortality-alert workflow moved advance care planning documentation from 3 of 8 patients to 3 of 7 (p = .999). A survey of 528 radiation oncology staff found AI knowledge scores differed by role. This suggests competencies vary by role, although the survey did not test any training approach.

Neither test reported enrolling Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. One study did not report its country. Whether role-specific training changes care equally across patient groups is unknown.

The CHAI frameworks and the FUTURE-AI consensus guideline call for training customized to end-user groups and for review of whether curricula address specialized roles. These are voluntary frameworks. The supplied sources cite no federal rule or state statute that requires role-specific AI training.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared role-tailored training with generic or no training using a concurrent control. None measured patient outcomes with adequate power, and none reported training cost, staff time, or how long any effect lasted.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither test reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups have no direct evidence on whether role-specific training changes how staff act on AI outputs for their patients.
